etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English concluden, borrowed from Latin conclūdere (“to shut up, close, end”).

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To end; to come to an end.

quote.citation: 1749, Henry Fielding, The History of Tom Jones, a Foundling:
quote.text: He inveighed against the folly of making oneself liable for the debts of others; vented many bitter execrations against the brother; and concluded with wishing something could be done for the unfortunate family.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To bring to an end; to close; to finish.

quote.citation: a. 1627 (date written), Francis [Bacon], “Considerations Touching a VVarre vvith Spaine. […]”, in William Rawley, editor, Certaine Miscellany VVorks of the Right Honourable Francis Lo. Verulam, Viscount S. Alban. […], London:  […]  I. Hauiland for Humphrey Robinson, […], published 1629, →OCLC:
quote.text: I will conclude this part with the speech of a counsellor of state.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To bring about as a result; to effect; to make.

quote.citation: 1591 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The First Part of Henry the Sixt”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene iv]:

definitions.definition: (transitive) To come to a conclusion, to a final decision.

quote.citation: a. 1694, John Tillotson, The Advantages of Religion to Societies:
quote.text: No man can certainly conclude God's love or hatred to any person by anything that befalls him.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To make a final determination or judgment concerning; to judge; to decide.

quote.text: But no frail man, however great or high, / Can be concluded blest before he die.

definitions.definition: (often passive voice) To shut off; to restrain; to limit; to estop; to bar.

quote.citation: a. 1677 (date written), Matthew Hale, The Primitive Origination of Mankind, Considered and Examined According to the Light of Nature, London:  […]  William Godbid, for William Shrowsbery, […], published 1677, →OCLC:
quote.text: If therefore they will appeal to revelation for their creation they must be concluded by it.

quote.citation: 1594–1597, Richard Hooker, edited by J[ohn] S[penser], Of the Lawes of Ecclesiastical Politie, […], London:  […]  Will[iam] Stansby [for Matthew Lownes], published 1611, →OCLC, (please specify the page):
quote.text: The very person of Christ [was] concluded within the grave.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To include; to comprehend; to shut up together; to embrace; to confine.

quote.citation: 1601, Ben Jonson, The Poetaster, act IV, scene VIII originally but scene VII in Gifford’s 1816 edition volume II, page 493:
quote.text: Banisht the Court? Let me be banisht Life; Since the chief end of Life is there concluded:Within the Court is all the Kingdom bounded,And as her sacred Sphear doth comprehendTen thousand times so much, as so much PlaceIn any part of all the Empire else;So every Body, moving in her Sphear,Contains Ten thousand times as much in him,As any other, her choice Orb excludes.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Romans 11:32:
quote.text: For God hath concluded all in unbelief.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Galatians 3:22:
quote.text: The Scripture hath concluded all under sin.

definitions.definition: (logic) to deduce, to infer (develop a causal relation)
